arguments.heading: What happened at the argument
paragraphs: Jeffrey Fisher argued that a defendant cannot lose Confrontation Clause rights by making a legitimate defense.
He stated this holds true even if the prosecution's hearsay contradicts that defense.
Ms. Mignola countered that the side that brought the case seeks a broad and sweeping rule.
She argued that a defendant can never open the door to evidence barred by the Confrontation Clause.

sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: This case tests the scope of the Confrontation Clause. It asks if a defendant can waive this constitutional protection by presenting a defense that conflicts with the prosecution's hearsay evidence.

sections.heading: What each side wants
paragraphs: the side that brought the case wants the Court to rule that a defendant never forfeits Confrontation Clause rights by opening the door to evidence.
the opposing side wants the Court to allow states to admit hearsay when a defendant's defense contradicts it.

sections.heading: What each side says
paragraphs: the side that brought the case argues that a legitimate defense based on admissible evidence cannot strip a defendant of the right to exclude testimonial hearsay.
the opposing side argues that a defendant can open the door to otherwise barred evidence by presenting a contradictory defense.

sections.heading: What the justices asked
paragraphs: Justice Sotomayor asked why the side that brought the case did not simply argue that the Reid precedent is unconstitutional.
Justice Alito questioned how the prosecution's evidence was admissible under state hearsay law despite the Confrontation Clause issues.

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: This case defines the limits of the Confrontation Clause. It determines whether defendants can strategically waive their right to cross-examine witnesses. The outcome shapes how courts handle contradictory evidence in criminal trials.
